title: MORAD: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Objective Rewards for RNA Inverse Design

paper.title: MORAD: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Objective Rewards for RNA Inverse Design
paper.abstract: Abstract We introduce MORAD, an online reinforcement learning framework for backbone-conditioned RNA diffusion models that trains a single shared policy across diverse target backbones. Structure-conditioned RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences compatible with a target three-dimensional backbone, yet existing reinforcement learning approaches either optimize a separate policy for each target backbone or rely on offline preference optimization, leaving online post-training of a reusable backbone-conditioned model largely unexplored. MORAD combines backbone-conditioned group sampling, group-relative reward normalization, and a forward-process diffusion objective. Beyond existing RL rewards that primarily target tertiary structural quality, MORAD jointly optimizes six measurements spanning tertiary geometry, base pairing, ensemble behavior, and sequence composition. To aggregate these heterogeneous objectives despite differences in scale and optimization direction, MORAD maps each measurement to a bounded desirability score and combines them with a weighted geometric mean. Compared with a tertiary-structure-only reward, this multi-objective formulation improves 10 of the 11 evaluation metrics that have a preferred direction. Applied to pretrained RIDE, MORAD improves GDT-TS by 16.0% (from 0.3300 to 0.3827) and pairing MCC by 19.4% (from 0.6110 to 0.7295), while reducing normalized ensemble defect by 27.5% (from 0.3906 to 0.2830). On the test set, MORAD outperforms RiboDiffusion, gRNAde, and RDesign across tertiary structural accuracy, secondary-structure pairing, and thermodynamic quality, establishing a new state of the art in structure-conditioned RNA inverse design.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: RNA inverse design generates nucleotide sequences that are compatible with a specified structure. Three-dimensional backbone conditioning makes local geometry and long-range spatial relationships available to a sequence generator. This formulation enables the construction of candidate RNAs for subsequent folding and functional evaluation. It also defines a one-to-many learning problem: a target backbone can admit multiple compatible sequences. Recent structure-conditioned methods therefore model a conditional sequence distribution and evaluate both structural compatibility and sequence recovery ( Joshi et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Tan et al., 2024 ) . Geometric learning and diffusion modeling provide complementary ways to represent this distribution. gRNAde encodes RNA backbones with geometric graph neural networks and supports multiple conformations ( Joshi et al., 2025 ) . RDesign exploits hierarchical representation learning to use limited structural data efficiently ( Tan et al., 2024 ) . RiboDiffusion combines structural conditioning with generative denoising, while RIDE provides a structure-conditioned diffusion backbone within the RIDER framework ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . These models establish a strong starting distribution for design. Post-training can then further improve these models using properties measured on their newly generated sequences. Reinforcement learning (RL) makes this feedback loop explicit. A design policy proposes candidates, a computational evaluator scores them, and the policy learns from the resulting rewards. LEARNA and Meta-LEARNA established this approach for secondary-structure-conditioned RNA design ( Runge et al., 2019 ) . More recent RNA methods investigate preference optimization, RL-guided diffusion, and step-wise latent optimization ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Si et al., 2026 ) . Protein design offers parallel evidence: EvoPlay combines self-play with sequence search, RL-DIF tunes structure-conditioned categorical diffusion, and ProteinZero updates inverse-folding models with online structural and stability feedback ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Ektefaie et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Together, these developments motivate learning a reusable design policy from feedback collected across many RNA backbones. Two coupled choices determine how such a policy learns. The first is the training interface. RNA feedback can involve a learned folding predictor, discrete base-pair comparisons, and thermodynamic software. An effective update rule must consume their scalar outputs while accommodating a multistep diffusion generator. Forward-process diffusion RL provides such an update rule through reward-weighted denoising objectives ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . The second choice is the reward itself. Tertiary alignment, pairing compatibility, and ensemble behavior describe different aspects of a design, with different units and scales. Their aggregation determines which candidate-level improvements the policy prioritizes. A structured reward should preserve these distinctions while producing an effective within-target learning signal. MORAD integrates these choices into a shared-policy RNA post-training workflow. For each target, an exponential-moving-average policy samples a group of sequences. Six measurements are mapped to bounded desirability scores, which a weighted geometric mean combines into a scalar reward. Group-relative normalization converts that reward into candidate weights for a DiffusionNFT-style update ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) . Training repeats across target backbones, and the resulting policy generates sequences directly from a new backbone at inference. Our contributions are: 1. A reusable RNA online RL framework. We formulate a shared-policy training procedure that connects structure-conditioned diffusion sampling, group-relative feedback, and forward-process optimization through modular interfaces. 2. A coordinated multi-objective reward. We specify six RNA design measurements, smooth desirability mappings, and weighted geometric aggregation, together with the data construction needed to support online scoring. 3. An improved shared RNA design model. We obtain MORAD by post-training RIDE and evaluate the same checkpoint across tertiary structure, secondary structure, and thermodynamics. On 153 evaluation targets, it reaches 0.3827 GDT-TS and 0.3400 TM-score. Held-out evaluations at 40 points during training track this improvement.

sections.heading: Conditioned RNA design.
sections.text: Secondary-structure-conditioned design uses pairing constraints to guide sequence search or learning. LEARNA trains a design agent, and Meta-LEARNA transfers experience across target structures ( Runge et al., 2019 ) . Three-dimensional conditioning adds backbone geometry: gRNAde develops geometric, multi-state sequence modeling; RDesign learns hierarchical structural representations; and RiboDiffusion generates sequences through conditional denoising ( Joshi et al., 2025 ; Tan et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) . RIDER combines its RIDE backbone with RL-guided optimization, optimizing and reporting one target backbone at a time, so the resulting weights are target-specific rather than reusable; SOLD studies step-wise optimization in a latent diffusion model ( Hu et al., 2026 ; Si et al., 2026 ) . RNA3DB groups RNA structures into structurally dissimilar components, providing a basis for assessing transfer across RNA structures ( Szikszai et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Reward-based learning for biomolecular sequences.
sections.text: Protein RL spans mutation search, language-model adaptation, and structure-conditioned generation. EvoPlay treats residue mutations as actions and couples a policy-value network with Monte Carlo tree search ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . KnowRLM incorporates biochemical knowledge into reinforced language models for directed evolution ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . RL-DIF optimizes a pretrained categorical diffusion model using structural consistency, with foldable diversity as an explicit evaluation goal ( Ektefaie et al., 2024 ) . ProteinZero uses online structural and stability proxies together with reference-policy and diversity regularization ( Wang et al., 2025b ) . DRAKES develops reward optimization for discrete diffusion with applications to DNA and protein design ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . For RNA, RiboPO constructs structure- and stability-aware preferences, complementing the online optimization routes explored by RIDER and SOLD ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Si et al., 2026 ) . Several methods train generative models from reward feedback. DDPO views reverse diffusion as a sequential decision process ( Black et al., 2024 ) . DRAKES propagates reward information through relaxed discrete sampling, while DiffusionNFT learns through the forward process using positive and negative denoising branches ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . GRPO provides a group-relative baseline for reward normalization ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . These mechanisms address distinct parts of the learning loop: trajectory optimization, reward propagation, and candidate-level credit assignment.

sections.heading: Multi-objective measurement and evaluation.
sections.text: Desirability functions map responses with different units onto a common scale; geometric aggregation is a classical construction for coordinating multiple responses ( Derringer & Suich, 1980 ) . RNA evaluation combines learned structural predictors such as RhoFold+, secondary-structure predictors such as EternaFold, and energy-based calculations from ViennaRNA ( Shen et al., 2024 ; Wayment-Steele et al., 2022 ; Lorenz et al., 2011 ) . US-align supports structural comparisons of nucleic acids ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) . RiboPO organizes evaluation across sequence, secondary structure, tertiary structure, and thermodynamics ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . Uncertainty estimates also complement aggregate RL scores ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) .

sections.heading: 3.2 Reward construction
sections.text: The reward combines six quantities with explicit roles. GDT-TS, TM-score, and RMSD assess the RhoFold+-predicted structure against the target backbone ( Shen et al., 2024 ) . Secondary-structure MCC measures agreement between the RNAfold structures of a candidate and its native reference ( Lorenz et al., 2011 ; Matthews, 1975 ) . Normalized ensemble defect measures expected nucleotide-level disagreement with that reference pairing under the candidate’s thermodynamic ensemble ( Zadeh et al., 2011 ) . A composition-deviation term compares candidate and native A/C/G/U frequencies. Appendix D.2 gives the measurement formulas and evaluation-tool configuration. For metric m j m_{j} , anchors a j a_{j} and b j b_{j} identify low and high desirability. We apply a clipped raised-cosine map, u j = clip ⁡ ( m j − a j b j − a j , 0 , 1 ) , d j = max ⁡ ( δ , 1 − cos ⁡ ( π ​ u j ) 2 ) , δ = 10 − 3 . u_{j}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{m_{j}-a_{j}}{b_{j}-a_{j}},0,1\right),\qquad d_{j}=\max\!\left(\delta,\frac{1-\cos(\pi u_{j})}{2}\right),\quad\delta=10^{-3}. (4) Lower-is-better measurements use b j < a j b_{j}<a_{j} . The anchors align units and specify the region where changes in a measurement affect the reward. Saturation limits the influence of extreme values, and the floor keeps logarithms finite. Geometric aggregation favors candidates that score reasonably on every measurement over candidates that excel on only one ( Derringer & Suich, 1980 ) . Above the desirability floor, ∂ log ⁡ R / ∂ d j = w ~ j / d j \partial\log R/\partial d_{j}=\widetilde{w}_{j}/d_{j} , so at a fixed weight the reward responds most strongly to the lowest scores. This property motivates the geometric form; it reaches the optimizer through the candidate weights r i r_{i} . Structural terms carry 85% of the nominal weight, while the three auxiliary terms still directly affect how candidates are ranked. With Eq. ( 1 ), normalization has two stages: desirability scores align the units and directions of the six measurements, and group-relative standardization removes difficulty differences between targets. sections.heading: 3.3 Data construction
sections.text: Each record stores a backbone X X , its native sequence y ⋆ y^{\star} , and a coordinate-validity mask. The backbone conditions generation, and the native sequence provides pairing and composition references during training; at inference the policy conditions on the target backbone alone. The training set contains 527 targets and the evaluation set 153. The evaluation set is built separately from the training set and comprises 71 RNA3DB entries, drawn from RNA3DB components that contain no training target, and 82 independently curated RCSB entries spanning 15–186 nucleotides ( Szikszai et al., 2024 ; Berman et al., 2000 ) . No evaluation sequence exactly matches a training sequence after normalization; each evaluation target’s maximum sequence identity to the training set has a median of 0.62, and Appendix C reports its full distribution. All 153 evaluation targets are used. Appendix C details preprocessing and screening.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: We initialize from pretrained RIDE and train for 390 updates over three epochs on four GPUs, using four target groups of eight candidates per update. The reported model is the final checkpoint, update 390; the held-out evaluations taken every ten updates document training and are not used to select a checkpoint. The 10.2M-parameter model uses an initial learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} with cosine decay to 0.3 times the initial rate. RhoFold+ scores tertiary structure ( Shen et al., 2024 ) ; Appendix D gives the configuration. Tables 1 and 2 compare MORAD with RiboDiffusion, gRNAde ( T = 0.1 T=0.1 ), RDesign, and pretrained RIDE using the first sampled candidate (candidate 0) for each of the 153 evaluation targets ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Joshi et al., 2025 ; Tan et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) ; the index is fixed for every model, with no best-of-eight selection. C1 ′ \prime TM has 126 valid targets; pairing counts vary by metric (Appendix D.1.1 ). Diversity uses all eight candidates per target (Appendix D.1.2 ); Table 3 reports a separate thermodynamic evaluation that also includes gRNAde ( T = 0.8 T=0.8 ). The checkpoint comparison (Appendix E ) and the training curves (Figure 3 ) come from separate evaluation runs.

sections.heading: 4.2 Comparison with existing RNA design models
sections.text: Across Tables 1 – 3 , MORAD attains the best mean on 14 of the 16 metrics with a preferred direction; the two exceptions, recovery and pLDDT, are led by RiboDiffusion.

sections.heading: 4.3 Reward design

To isolate this choice, we post-train two policies from the same pretrained RIDE using the same data, optimizer, and schedule, and change only the reward: a structural-only reward of the kind used by existing work, and the MORAD reward. sections.heading: Effect of the auxiliary terms.
sections.text: Although the auxiliary terms carry only 15% of the nominal weight, the MORAD reward also improves the shared tertiary scores: geometric aggregation lowers the reward of candidates that align well but pair poorly.

sections.heading: 4.4 Held-out performance during training
sections.text: We evaluate the held-out targets every tenth update, giving 40 measurements from update 0 to 390 (Figure 3 ). GDT-TS increases from 0.3365 to 0.3711 and C4 ′ \prime TM from 0.2912 to 0.3296: relative gains of 10.3% and 13.2%. These values come from the held-out evaluations run during training; Table 1 is a separate, final evaluation of update 390.

sections.heading: Candidate variation.
sections.text: During training, within-target sequence diversity decreases from 0.2023 to 0.1616. In the final eight-candidate evaluation, MORAD has Hamming and 3-mer diversity of 0.2344 and 0.3673, versus RIDE’s 0.2971 and 0.5270; Appendix D.1.2 gives all models. This quality–diversity tradeoff is well-documented in language-model RL and protein inverse folding ( Kirk et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2025 ; Ektefaie et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) , motivating joint reporting of both dimensions. Figure 3: Structural-score trends over all 40 evaluations. Thick lines show a centered five-point moving average; faint traces show the raw held-out scores recorded during training, with one sampled candidate per target. Near the two ends, the average uses only the available points. Table 10 reports the evaluation of the last checkpoint, update 390. Appendix E.1 defines the smoothing.

sections.heading: 5 Limitations
sections.text: The experiments evaluate MORAD on a single 10.2M-parameter RIDE backbone, demonstrating the framework on a compact model; the same modular interfaces accommodate larger structure-conditioned backbones. Reward scoring and tertiary evaluation both use the RhoFold+ predictor, consistent with current RNA design RL practice ( Hu et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2024 ) ; experimental structural validation remains a separate step beyond the scope of this computational study. The reward also covers equilibrium folding properties, leaving kinetics and function-specific objectives as future additions to the reward.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: MORAD establishes a shared-policy online post-training workflow for RNA design, integrating target-relative feedback, six-component rewards, and forward-process diffusion optimization. The last checkpoint of the completed run (update 390) reaches mean scores of 0.3827 GDT-TS and 0.3400 TM-score in the final evaluation. Together with the pairing and ensemble-defect results and the full training trajectory, these results document the quality gains and multi-objective tradeoffs of online post-training.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This is a computational study. It uses publicly available RNA structures from RNA3DB and the PDB and involves no human subjects, no animal experiments, and no new laboratory measurements ( Szikszai et al., 2024 ; Berman et al., 2000 ) . Designed sequences are computational candidates scored by folding and thermodynamic software; none were synthesized or assayed, and we make no functional, therapeutic, or biosafety claims for them.

sections.heading: Records and screening.
sections.text: Each record contains a native sequence, its source PDB chain, backbone coordinates, and a coordinate-validity mask. Screening folds the native sequence with RhoFold+ and keeps targets whose prediction reaches C4 ′ \prime GDT-TS of at least 0.30 under centered, index-preserving Kabsch alignment ( Kabsch, 1976 ) .

sections.heading: Fixed splits.
sections.text: The training set has 527 targets of length 27–258 nt (median 75); the evaluation set has 153 targets of length 15–186 nt (median 65). Evaluation sources comprise 71 RNA3DB entries, drawn from RNA3DB components that contain no training target, and 82 entries curated from RCSB ( Szikszai et al., 2024 ; Berman et al., 2000 ) . All 153 are used for evaluation. When the native sequences are folded with RhoFold+, the median GDT-TS is 0.6400 for the training set and 0.6014 for the evaluation set.

sections.heading: Train–test separation.
sections.text: The two sets are built independently. Character-wise and MD5 checks report no exact match between the 153 normalized evaluation sequences and the 527 training sequences. To characterize the residual similarity that remains after exact-duplicate removal, we compute each evaluation target’s maximum global identity to the training set under Needleman–Wunsch alignment ( Needleman & Wunsch, 1970 ) . The median is 0.6207 and the mean 0.6615; 26 of the 153 targets reach 0.80, including 12 that reach 0.95; at the pair level, however, only 64 of the 80,631 evaluation–training pairs (0.08%) reach 0.80. All 153 targets are kept, with no exclusion based on similarity or results. Both policies in Table 4 are trained on the same training set and evaluated on the same evaluation set, so the reward comparison holds this residual similarity fixed.

sections.heading: Reference use.
sections.text: Backbones and masks condition generation. Native RNAfold pairings and nucleotide frequencies provide training references. Pairing evaluation uses base pairs extracted from the native 3D structures, available for 137 targets; the other 16 short RNAs have no pairing reference and remain in the tertiary, recovery, and thermodynamic evaluations.

Affiliation: Fudan University Abstract We introduce MORAD, an online reinforcement learning framework for backbone-conditioned RNA diffusion models that trains a single shared policy across diverse target backbones. Structure-conditioned RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences compatible with a target three-dimensional backbone, yet existing reinforcement learning approaches either optimize a separate policy for each target backbone or rely on offline preference optimization, leaving online post-training of a reusable backbone-conditioned model largely unexplored. MORAD combines backbone-conditioned group sampling, group-relative reward normalization, and a forward-process diffusion objective. Beyond existing RL rewards that primarily target tertiary structural quality, MORAD jointly optimizes six measurements spanning tertiary geometry, base pairing, ensemble behavior, and sequence composition. To aggregate these heterogeneous objectives despite differences in scale and optimization direction, MORAD maps each measurement to a bounded desirability score and combines them with a weighted geometric mean. Compared with a tertiary-structure-only reward, this multi-objective formulation improves 10 of the 11 evaluation metrics that have a preferred direction. Applied to pretrained RIDE, MORAD improves GDT-TS by 16.0% (from 0.3300 to 0.3827) and pairing MCC by 19.4% (from 0.6110 to 0.7295), while reducing normalized ensemble defect by 27.5% (from 0.3906 to 0.2830). On the test set, MORAD outperforms RiboDiffusion, gRNAde, and RDesign across tertiary structural accuracy, secondary-structure pairing, and thermodynamic quality, establishing a new state of the art in structure-conditioned RNA inverse design. † † footnotetext: Project page: https://gabrile166.github.io/MORAD/ 1 Introduction RNA inverse design generates nucleotide sequences that are compatible with a specified structure. Three-dimensional backbone conditioning makes local geometry and long-range spatial relationships available to a sequence generator. This formulation enables the construction of candidate RNAs for subsequent folding and functional evaluation. It also defines a one-to-many learning problem: a target backbone can admit multiple compatible sequences. Recent structure-conditioned methods therefore model a conditional sequence distribution and evaluate both structural compatibility and sequence recovery ( Joshi et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Tan et al., 2024 ) . Geometric learning and diffusion modeling provide complementary ways to represent this distribution. gRNAde encodes RNA backbones with geometric graph neural networks and supports multiple conformations ( Joshi et al., 2025 ) . RDesign exploits hierarchical representation learning to use limited structural data efficiently ( Tan et al., 2024 ) . RiboDiffusion combines structural conditioning with generative denoising, while RIDE provides a structure-conditioned diffusion backbone within the RIDER framework ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . These models establish a strong starting distribution for design. Post-training can then further improve these models using properties measured on their newly generated sequences. Reinforcement learning (RL) makes this feedback loop explicit. A design policy proposes candidates, a computational evaluator scores them, and the policy learns from the resulting rewards. LEARNA and Meta-LEARNA established this approach for secondary-structure-conditioned RNA design ( Runge et al., 2019 ) . More recent RNA methods investigate preference optimization, RL-guided diffusion, and step-wise latent optimization ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Si et al., 2026 ) . Protein design offers parallel evidence: EvoPlay combines self-play with sequence search, RL-DIF tunes structure-conditioned categorical diffusion, and ProteinZero updates inverse-folding models with online structural and stability feedback ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Ektefaie et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Together, these developments motivate learning a reusable design policy from feedback collected across many RNA backbones. Two coupled choices determine how such a policy learns. The first is the training interface. RNA feedback can involve a learned folding predictor, discrete base-pair comparisons, and thermodynamic software. An effective update rule must consume their scalar outputs while accommodating a multistep diffusion generator. Forward-process diffusion RL provides such an update rule through reward-weighted denoising objectives ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . The second choice is the reward itself. Tertiary alignment, pairing compatibility, and ensemble behavior describe different aspects of a design, with different units and scales. Their aggregation determines which candidate-level improvements the policy prioritizes. A structured reward should preserve these distinctions while producing an effective within-target learning signal. MORAD integrates these choices into a shared-policy RNA post-training workflow. For each target, an exponential-moving-average policy samples a group of sequences. Six measurements are mapped to bounded desirability scores, which a weighted geometric mean combines into a scalar reward. Group-relative normalization converts that reward into candidate weights for a DiffusionNFT-style update ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) . Training repeats across target backbones, and the resulting policy generates sequences directly from a new backbone at inference. Our contributions are: 1. A reusable RNA online RL framework. We formulate a shared-policy training procedure that connects structure-conditioned diffusion sampling, group-relative feedback, and forward-process optimization through modular interfaces. 2. A coordinated multi-objective reward. We specify six RNA design measurements, smooth desirability mappings, and weighted geometric aggregation, together with the data construction needed to support online scoring. 3. An improved shared RNA design model. We obtain MORAD by post-training RIDE and evaluate the same checkpoint across tertiary structure, secondary structure, and thermodynamics. On 153 evaluation targets, it reaches 0.3827 GDT-TS and 0.3400 TM-score. Held-out evaluations at 40 points during training track this improvement. 2 Related work Conditioned RNA design. Secondary-structure-conditioned design uses pairing constraints to guide sequence search or learning. LEARNA trains a design agent, and Meta-LEARNA transfers experience across target structures ( Runge et al., 2019 ) . Three-dimensional conditioning adds backbone geometry: gRNAde develops geometric, multi-state sequence modeling; RDesign learns hierarchical structural representations; and RiboDiffusion generates sequences through conditional denoising ( Joshi et al., 2025 ; Tan et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) . RIDER combines its RIDE backbone with RL-guided optimization, optimizing and reporting one target backbone at a time, so the resulting weights are target-specific rather than reusable; SOLD studies step-wise optimization in a latent diffusion model ( Hu et al., 2026 ; Si et al., 2026 ) . RNA3DB groups RNA structures into structurally dissimilar components, providing a basis for assessing transfer across RNA structures ( Szikszai et al., 2024 ) . Reward-based learning for biomolecular sequences. Protein RL spans mutation search, language-model adaptation, and structure-conditioned generation. EvoPlay treats residue mutations as actions and couples a policy-value network with Monte Carlo tree search ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . KnowRLM incorporates biochemical knowledge into reinforced language models for directed evolution ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . RL-DIF optimizes a pretrained categorical diffusion model using structural consistency, with foldable diversity as an explicit evaluation goal ( Ektefaie et al., 2024 ) . ProteinZero uses online structural and stability proxies together with reference-policy and diversity regularization ( Wang et al., 2025b ) . DRAKES develops reward optimization for discrete diffusion with applications to DNA and protein design ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . For RNA, RiboPO constructs structure- and stability-aware preferences, complementing the online optimization routes explored by RIDER and SOLD ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Si et al., 2026 ) . Several methods train generative models from reward feedback. DDPO views reverse diffusion as a sequential decision process ( Black et al., 2024 ) . DRAKES propagates reward information through relaxed discrete sampling, while DiffusionNFT learns through the forward process using positive and negative denoising branches ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . GRPO provides a group-relative baseline for reward normalization ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . These mechanisms address distinct parts of the learning loop: trajectory optimization, reward propagation, and candidate-level credit assignment. Multi-objective measurement and evaluation. Desirability functions map responses with different units onto a common scale; geometric aggregation is a classical construction for coordinating multiple responses ( Derringer & Suich, 1980 ) . RNA evaluation combines learned structural predictors such as RhoFold+, secondary-structure predictors such as EternaFold, and energy-based calculations from ViennaRNA ( Shen et al., 2024 ; Wayment-Steele et al., 2022 ; Lorenz et al., 2011 ) . US-align supports structural comparisons of nucleic acids ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) . RiboPO organizes evaluation across sequence, secondary structure, tertiary structure, and thermodynamics ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . Uncertainty estimates also complement aggregate RL scores ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) . 3 Method 3.1 Online training algorithm and optimization objective Let X X denote an RNA backbone with L L valid nucleotide positions and let y ∈ { A , C , G , U } L y\in\{A,C,G,U\}^{L} denote a designed sequence. Reward scoring and tertiary evaluation both use the RhoFold+ predictor, consistent with current RNA design RL practice ( Hu et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2024 ) ; experimental structural validation remains a separate step beyond the scope of this computational study. The reward also covers equilibrium folding properties, leaving kinetics and function-specific objectives as future additions to the reward. 6 Conclusion MORAD establishes a shared-policy online post-training workflow for RNA design, integrating target-relative feedback, six-component rewards, and forward-process diffusion optimization. The last checkpoint of the completed run (update 390) reaches mean scores of 0.3827 GDT-TS and 0.3400 TM-score in the final evaluation. Together with the pairing and ensemble-defect results and the full training trajectory, these results document the quality gains and multi-objective tradeoffs of online post-training.
